title:
The lords rise at Cao Cao's forged edict
Three heroes break the pass and fight Lü Bu
paragraphs:
Now [Chen Gong](char-chen-gong) was at the point of striking [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) dead when his thought turned. "I followed him here for the country's sake, and to kill him now would be a wrong. Better leave him and go elsewhere." He sheathed his sword, mounted, and rode for Dong Commandery without waiting for the light. Cao Cao woke, and Chen Gong was not there. "He thinks me a hard man for what I said, and has gone," he said within himself. "I must get on and stay here no more." So he rode through the night to [Chenliu](loc-chenliu), found his father, and told him all that had passed; he would spend the family wealth, he said, to raise a righteous army. "Our means are too small, and I fear it will not do," said his father. "There is a man here raised [Xiaolian](misc-xiaolian), Wei Hong, open-handed and staunch for the right, and his house is immensely rich. If he will help, the design can go forward."
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) set out wine and spread a feast, and asked Wei Hong to the house with all courtesy. He said: "The house of Han is without a master, and [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) holds all the power, cheating his sovereign and harming the people, till the whole realm grinds its teeth at him. I would put out my strength to uphold the altars of the land, but the strength is not in me. You are a loyal and upright man, and I make bold to ask your help." Wei Hong said: "I have had that mind in me this long while, and only grieved that I had met no hero. Since Mengde has so great a purpose, my whole fortune is at your service." Cao Cao was overjoyed. He sent the forged edict out first, by fast riders to every quarter, and then set about raising his righteous army, putting up a white banner for the recruiting with the two words Loyalty and Righteousness upon it. Within a few days the men who answered came thronging thick as rain.
One day there came to join [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) a man of Weiguo in Yangping, [Yue Jin](char-yue-jin) by name, Wenqian by style; and after him a man of Julu in Shanyang, [Li Dian](char-li-dian) by name, Mancheng by style. Cao Cao kept them both for officers of his own tent. There came also a man of Qiao in the Principality of Pei, [Xiahou Dun](char-xiahou-dun), styled Yuanrang, descended from [Xiahou Ying](char-xiahou-ying). From a boy he had worked at spear and staff, and at fourteen he went to a master to learn arms; a man spoke foully of his master, and Xiahou Dun killed him and fled away out of the district. Hearing now that Cao Cao was raising troops, he came in with his younger cousin [Xiahou Yuan](char-xiahou-yuan), each of them bringing a thousand stout fellows. These two were Cao Cao's own cousins, for his father [Cao Song](char-cao-song) was born a son of the Xiahou house and passed by adoption into the Cao family.
Within a few days two of his own clan, [Cao Ren](char-cao-ren) and [Cao Hong](char-cao-hong), came to his help with above a thousand men apiece. Cao Ren's style was Zixiao and Cao Hong's Zilian, and both were practised in the handling of troops and thoroughly expert at arms. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) was well pleased, and mustered and drilled his companies in the village. Wei Hong brought out the whole of his fortune for clothing and armor, flags and banners, and grain came in from every quarter past all counting.
By this time [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) had [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao)'s forged edict, and he gathered his officers, civil and military, and came from [Bohai](loc-bohai) with thirty thousand men to swear alliance with him. Cao Cao drew up a call to arms and sent it round the commanderies. It ran: "Cao Cao and his fellows make this proclamation to the realm in the great cause. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) cheats Heaven and defrauds Earth. He has brought a kingdom to ruin and murdered his sovereign, defiled the forbidden palace and butchered the living; wolfish and pitiless, he has heaped crime upon crime! We hold now a secret edict from the Son of Heaven, and gather a great righteous army, sworn to sweep the Middle Kingdom clean and cut down the whole brood of villains. Raise your righteous armies, and vent with us the wrath of all men. Uphold the royal house and save the common people. On the day this reaches you, act upon it with speed!"
When the call to arms had gone out, the lords of the garrisons rose in answer to it. The first was [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu), General of the Rear and Grand Administrator of Nanyang. The second, [Han Fu](char-han-fu), Inspector of [Ji Province](loc-ji-province). The third, [Kong Zhou](char-kong-zhou), Inspector of [Yu Province](loc-yu-province). The fourth, [Liu Dai](char-liu-dai), Inspector of [Yan Province](loc-yan-province). The fifth, [Wang Kuang](char-wang-kuang), Grand Administrator of Henei Commandery. The sixth, [Zhang Miao](char-zhang-miao), Grand Administrator of [Chenliu](loc-chenliu). The seventh, [Qiao Mao](char-qiao-mao), Grand Administrator of Dong Commandery. The eighth, [Yuan Yi](char-yuan-yi), Grand Administrator of Shanyang. The ninth, [Bao Xin](char-bao-xin), Chancellor of Jibei. The tenth, [Kong Rong](char-kong-rong), Grand Administrator of Beihai. The eleventh, [Zhang Chao](char-zhang-chao), Grand Administrator of Guangling. The twelfth, [Tao Qian](char-tao-qian), Inspector of [Xu Province](loc-xu-province). The thirteenth, [Ma Teng](char-ma-teng), Grand Administrator of Xiliang. The fourteenth, [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan), Grand Administrator of Beiping. The fifteenth, [Zhang Yang](char-zhang-yang), Grand Administrator of Shangdang. The sixteenth, [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian), Marquis of Wucheng and Grand Administrator of Changsha. The seventeenth, [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), Marquis of Qi and Grand Administrator of [Bohai](loc-bohai). Their forces were of unequal strength, some thirty thousand and some ten or twenty thousand, and each came on toward [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) with his own officers.
Now [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan), Grand Administrator of Beiping, was leading fifteen thousand picked men by way of Pingyuan County in Dezhou. As he went he saw far off, among a clump of mulberries, a yellow banner and a few horsemen riding out to meet him; and when he looked, it was [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei). "How do you come to be here, brother?" said Gongsun Zan. "It was by your recommendation, brother, that I was made Magistrate of Pingyuan," said Liu Bei. "Hearing that your army was passing this way I came out to wait on you. Come into the city and rest your horses." Gongsun Zan pointed at [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei). "And who are these?" "Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, my sworn brothers," said Liu Bei. "The same who broke the Yellow Turbans with you?" "It was all their doing." "And what posts have they now?" "Guan Yu is a mounted archer, and Zhang Fei an archer on foot," said Liu Bei. Gongsun Zan sighed. "Here are heroes buried out of sight! [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) is in revolt, and the lords of the realm are going up together to destroy him. Throw up this mean little office, brother, and come with us against the traitor and put out your strength for the house of Han. What do you say?" "I will go gladly," said Liu Bei. Zhang Fei said: "If you had let me kill the traitor that time, we should have been spared this day's work." "What is done is done," said Guan Yu. "Let us get ready and be off."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) rode with a few horsemen in [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan)'s train, and [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) met them. The rest of the lords came in one after another, and each pitched his camp, till the lines ran above two hundred li. Cao Cao killed oxen and horses for a great gathering of them all, and they took counsel how they should advance. [Wang Kuang](char-wang-kuang), the Grand Administrator, said: "We are met in the great cause, and a chief of the alliance must be set up. Let all take his orders, and then march." Cao Cao said: "Four generations of [Yuan Benchu](char-yuan-shao)'s house have sat among the [Three Ducal Ministers](misc-three-ducal-ministers), and his gate is full of men who served under them of old. He comes of famous ministers of Han, and may be chief of the alliance." [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) refused again and again. "None but Benchu will do," they all said, and then he consented. Next day a platform of three tiers was raised, with the banners of the five directions ranged about it and above them the white yak-tail standard and the yellow axe, the tallies of command and the general's seal. Then Yuan Shao was asked to go up. He set his robes straight, girded on his sword, and climbed with a solemn air, burned incense, and bowed twice. The oath ran: "Misfortune is upon the house of Han, and the imperial order has lost its hold. The traitor [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) has seized his chance upon our divisions to work ruin, bringing calamity on the Sovereign and loosing cruelty over the people. We, Yuan Shao and the rest, fearing that the altars of the land may be lost, have banded our righteous troops together and come as one to the country's need. We who are sworn in this bond shall be of one heart and strain together, to do a subject's duty and keep no second purpose. Whoever breaks this oath, let his life be struck from him and no seed of his remain. Let August Heaven and Sovereign Earth and the bright spirits of our forefathers be witness to it!"
The reading done, they smeared their lips with the blood of the sacrifice. The words had been so fervent that tears ran down every face. When the blood rite was over they came down from the platform, and the company helped [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) to the chief seat in the tent, the rest taking their places in two rows by rank and years. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) sent the wine round several times, and said: "Now that we have a chief of the alliance, let every man take his orders and uphold the state together, with no reckoning of strong and weak." Yuan Shao said: "I am a man of no great parts, but since you gentlemen have raised me to be chief of the alliance, merit shall have its reward and fault its punishment. The state has its standing penalties and an army its discipline. Let every man keep them, and none transgress." "In everything we obey you," they all said. Yuan Shao said: "My brother [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu) shall have charge of the grain and forage, and see every camp supplied, so that none goes short. We need a man besides to lead the van, go straight down to [Sishui Pass](loc-sishui-pass) and offer battle. The rest will hold the strong ground and stand ready behind him." [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian), Grand Administrator of Changsha, stepped out. "Let me lead the van." "Wentai is bold and fiery, and the charge is his," said Yuan Shao. So Sun Jian took his own men and horse and drove down upon Sishui Pass. The officers holding the pass sent a fast courier to the Chancellor's residence in [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) with word of their danger. [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), since all power had come into his hands, had feasted every day. [Li Ru](char-li-ru) took the dispatch and brought it straight to him. Dong Zhuo was alarmed, and called his generals together in haste. [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu), Marquis of Wen, stepped forward. "Rest easy, father. I look on the lords beyond the pass as chaff. Let me lead out an army of tigers and wolves, and I will have the heads off them all and hang them at the capital gate." "Having Fengxian, I may sleep easy!" said Dong Zhuo, delighted. Scarce had he spoken when a man behind Lü Bu called out: "Why use an ox-knife to kill a chicken? There is no need to trouble the Marquis to go himself. I will fetch you the heads of all those lords as easily as a man takes something out of a bag." Dong Zhuo turned and looked. The man stood nine chi, with a tiger's body and a wolf's loins, a leopard's head and an ape's arms, a man from west of the passes, Hua by surname and [Xiong](char-hua-xiong) by name. Dong Zhuo heard him gladly, made him Colonel of Cavalry, gave him fifty thousand horse and foot, and sent him with [Li Su](char-li-su), Hu Zhen and Zhao Cen to ride through the night to the pass and meet the enemy. Among the lords was [Bao Xin](char-bao-xin), Chancellor of Jibei, who thought to himself that with Sun Jian in the van the first honors would go to him, and sent his brother [Bao Zhong](char-bao-zhong) off secretly with three thousand horse and foot by a byway, straight down to the foot of the pass to challenge them. [Hua Xiong](char-hua-xiong) came flying down with five hundred mailed horsemen, shouting: "Stand, you rebel!" Bao Zhong turned in haste to fall back, but Hua Xiong's hand rose, the blade fell, and he was cut out of the saddle. Many of his officers were taken alive. Hua Xiong sent Bao Zhong's head to the Chancellor's residence with news of the victory, and Dong Zhuo made him a Commander.
[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) came up before the pass with four generals of his own. The first was [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu), styled Demou, a man of Tuyin in Youbeiping, who carried an iron-spined serpent spear. The second, [Huang Gai](char-huang-gai), styled Gongfu, a man of Lingling, with an iron mace. The third, [Han Dang](char-han-dang), styled Yigong, a man of Lingzhi in Liaoxi, with a great blade. The fourth, [Zu Mao](char-zu-mao), styled Darong, a man of Fuchun in Wu Commandery, with a pair of blades. Sun Jian wore a coat of bright silver mail and a red headcloth, and sat a horse with a flowered mane, his Ancient Ingot Blade laid across the saddle. He pointed up at the pass and railed at them: "You knaves that take a traitor's part, why not yield at once!"
Hu Zhen, [Hua Xiong](char-hua-xiong)'s lieutenant, came out of the pass with five thousand men to give battle. [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu) put his horse to the gallop, levelled his spear and made straight for him; they had not fought a few bouts when the point took Hu Zhen in the throat and he fell dead from the saddle. [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) waved his army on and drove right up to the pass, but arrows and stones came down from above like rain, and he drew his men back and camped at Liangdong, sending word of the victory to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) and pressing [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu) for grain. Someone said to Yuan Shu: "Sun Jian is the fierce tiger of [Jiangdong](loc-jiangdong). If he breaks into [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) and kills [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), we shall only have rid ourselves of a wolf to get a tiger. Send him no grain, and his army will break up of itself." Yuan Shu listened and sent out neither grain nor forage. Food ran short in Sun Jian's camp and his men fell into disorder, and spies carried word of it up to the pass. [Li Su](char-li-su) laid a plan before Hua Xiong: "Tonight let me take a force down by a byway and fall upon the back of Sun Jian's camp, while you drive at the front of it, General. Sun Jian will be taken."
[Hua Xiong](char-hua-xiong) agreed, and gave the order for the men to eat their fill and go down from the pass under cover of night. The moon was bright and the wind clear. It was midnight when they came to [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian)'s camp, and they drove straight in with drums and shouting. Sun Jian flung on his armor in haste, got to horse, and ran full upon Hua Xiong. The two closed, and they had not fought a few bouts when [Li Su](char-li-su)'s force came up behind and set the fires going. Sun Jian's men scattered in confusion; his generals were each left fighting where they stood, and only [Zu Mao](char-zu-mao) kept close to him as the two broke out through the ring and rode. Hua Xiong came after them. Sun Jian took his arrows and loosed two, one after the other, and Hua Xiong dodged them both; he was drawing for the third when he pulled too hard and snapped his magpie-figured bow, and had to throw it away and ride for it. Zu Mao said: "The red headcloth on your head catches the eye, my lord, and the rebels know you by it. Take it off and let me wear it." So Sun Jian took it off and put on Zu Mao's helmet, and the two parted and rode different ways. Hua Xiong's men kept after the red headcloth only, and Sun Jian got clear by a byway. Zu Mao, hard pressed, hung the headcloth on a courtyard post of a house that the fire had not wholly consumed, and slipped into the wood to hide.
[Hua Xiong](char-hua-xiong)'s men saw the red headcloth from afar in the moonlight and ringed it round on every side, not daring to come near. They shot arrows at it, and so found out the trick, and went up and took it. Then [Zu Mao](char-zu-mao) broke out from behind the trees, swinging his two blades to cut Hua Xiong down; but Hua Xiong gave a great shout, and with one stroke brought him out of the saddle. The killing went on till daybreak, and then Hua Xiong led his men back up to the pass. [Cheng Pu](char-cheng-pu), [Huang Gai](char-huang-gai) and [Han Dang](char-han-dang) all found their way back to [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian), who gathered his men together again and made his camp. He grieved without ceasing for the loss of Zu Mao, and sent a man through the night to carry word to [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao). "I never thought [Sun Wentai](char-sun-jian) would be beaten by Hua Xiong!" said Yuan Shao, dismayed, and he called the lords together to take counsel. They all came, [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) last of them, and Yuan Shao had him in and seated with the rest. Yuan Shao said: "The other day [General Bao](char-bao-xin)'s brother pushed forward on his own against orders, and threw his life away with a great many of our men. Now Sun Wentai too is beaten by Hua Xiong. Our ardor is blunted. What is to be done?" None of the lords spoke.
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) lifted his eyes and looked round the company, and saw three men standing behind [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan), of uncommon aspect, all of them smiling coldly where they stood. "Who are those behind you, Grand Administrator?" he asked. Gongsun Zan called [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) out. "This is a brother of mine from boyhood, when we lodged together at our books: Liu Bei, Magistrate of Pingyuan." "Is this not the [Liu Xuande](char-liu-bei) who broke the Yellow Turbans?" said [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao). "It is," said Gongsun Zan, and bade Liu Bei make his bow; and then he told them at length what Liu Bei had done and of what house he came. Yuan Shao said: "Since he is of the imperial line, bring a seat." And he bade him sit. Liu Bei would have declined it. Yuan Shao said: "It is not your name or your rank I honor, but that you are of the Emperor's own stock." So Liu Bei took the lowest seat, and [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) stood behind him with folded hands.
A scout came in suddenly with word: "[Hua Xiong](char-hua-xiong) has come down from the pass with his mailed horse, and carries [Grand Administrator Sun](char-sun-jian)'s red headcloth on a long pole; he is before the camp, railing at us and offering battle." "Who will go out against him?" said [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao). Yu She, a bold officer, stepped out from behind [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu). "Let me go." Yuan Shao was pleased, and sent him out; and word came back at once that Yu She had not fought three bouts with Hua Xiong before Hua Xiong cut him down. They were all taken aback. [Han Fu](char-han-fu), the Grand Administrator, said: "I have a champion named Pan Feng, who can kill Hua Xiong." Yuan Shao sent him out at once, and Pan Feng took up his great axe and mounted. He had not been gone long when a rider came flying back with the news that Pan Feng too was cut down by Hua Xiong. The color went out of every face. "A pity my two chief generals [Yan Liang](char-yan-liang) and [Wen Chou](char-wen-chou) are not yet come!" said Yuan Shao. "With one of them here, what should I fear from Hua Xiong?" He had not done speaking when a man below the steps cried out: "Let me go and bring you Hua Xiong's head here before the tent!" They looked, and saw a man nine chi tall with a beard of two chi, the eyes of a red phoenix and brows like silkworms at rest, a face like a ripe date and a voice like a great bell, standing before the tent. Yuan Shao asked who he was. "That is [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu), [Liu Xuande](char-liu-bei)'s brother," said [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan). Yuan Shao asked what post he held. "He follows Liu Xuande as a mounted archer." Yuan Shu roared at him from his seat: "Do you take us for lords with no great general? A mere archer dares talk so wildly! Throw him out!" [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) stopped him quickly. "Be easy, Gonglu. The man would not talk so big without courage and skill behind it. Let him try a ride, and if he does not win, there will be time enough to call him to account." Yuan Shao said: "Send out an archer to fight, and Hua Xiong will laugh at us for it." "The man's bearing is nothing common," said Cao Cao. "How should Hua Xiong know he is an archer?" Guan Yu said: "If I do not win, take my head."
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) had a cup of wine warmed and poured for [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) to drink before he mounted. "Pour it out and let it stand," said Guan Yu. "I shall be back straightway." He went out of the tent, took up his blade, and sprang to the saddle. The lords heard the drums thunder beyond the pass and a great shout go up, as though heaven were breaking and the earth falling in, the peaks shaking and the hills coming down, and fear took them all. Before they could send for news, the bridle bells rang out, the horse came in to the central camp, and Guan Yu threw [Hua Xiong](char-hua-xiong)'s head down on the ground. The wine was still warm. A later poet praised him:
> The first of feats, by heav'n and earth extolled;
> Before the camp the painted drums were rolled.
> Guan Yu set by his cup and proved his arm;
> He slew Hua Xiong, and still the wine was warm.
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) was greatly pleased. [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) came out from behind [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) and shouted: "My brother has killed [Hua Xiong](char-hua-xiong)! Why not cut our way through the pass this minute and take [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) alive? What are we waiting for!" [Yuan Shu](char-yuan-shu) flew into a rage. "We great ministers hold ourselves back, and a little trooper under a county magistrate dares swagger! Put the whole lot of them out of the tent!" "Reward the man who does the work," said Cao Cao. "What has high or low to do with it?" Yuan Shu said: "Since you gentlemen think so much of a county magistrate, I will take my leave." "Shall one word spoil the great business?" said Cao Cao; and he bade [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) take Liu Bei, [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and Zhang Fei back to their camp for the time. The officers all dispersed, and Cao Cao sent a man secretly with beef and wine to comfort the three. Meanwhile the beaten remnant of Hua Xiong's men carried word up to the pass, and [Li Su](char-li-su) wrote an urgent dispatch in haste and sent it in to Dong Zhuo, who called [Li Ru](char-li-ru) and [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) and the rest together to take counsel. Li Ru said: "We have lost our general Hua Xiong, and the rebels are strong. [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) is chief of their alliance, and his uncle [Yuan Wei](char-yuan-wei) is Grand Tutor here. Should the two work together, we shall be in grave danger, and we had best remove him first. Lead the great army out yourself, Chancellor, and divide it to hunt them down."
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) thought well of it, and called [Li Jue](char-li-jue) and [Guo Si](char-guo-si) to take five hundred men and ring the house of [Yuan Wei](char-yuan-wei) the Grand Tutor; and they killed every soul in it, old and young alike, and Yuan Wei's head went first to the pass to be shown there. Then Dong Zhuo raised two hundred thousand men and came on by two roads. By the one he sent Li Jue and Guo Si ahead with fifty thousand to hold [Sishui Pass](loc-sishui-pass) and give no battle; he took a hundred and fifty thousand himself, with [Li Ru](char-li-ru), [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu), [Fan Chou](char-fan-chou) and [Zhang Ji](char-zhang-ji), to hold [Hulao Pass](loc-hulao-pass), which lies fifty li from [Luoyang](loc-luoyang). When the army came up, Dong Zhuo ordered Lü Bu to pitch a great camp before the pass with thirty thousand men, while he lay upon the pass himself.
Scouts on fast horses carried word into [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao)'s great camp, and he called the company to counsel. [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) said: "[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) has his army at [Hulao](loc-hulao-pass), and cuts our line across the middle. Half our force should be drawn off to meet him." So Yuan Shao told off eight of the lords — [Wang Kuang](char-wang-kuang), [Qiao Mao](char-qiao-mao), [Bao Xin](char-bao-xin), [Yuan Yi](char-yuan-yi), [Kong Rong](char-kong-rong), [Zhang Yang](char-zhang-yang), [Tao Qian](char-tao-qian) and [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) — to go against him at Hulao Pass, while Cao Cao moved to and fro with his own men to support them. The eight set out, each with his own force, and Wang Kuang, Grand Administrator of Henei, came up first. [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) came flying to meet him with three thousand mailed horse. Wang Kuang drew his men into line of battle and reined in under the standard to look, and Lü Bu rode out before his own line: on his head a three-pronged coronet of purple gold binding his hair, a battle robe of red Xichuan brocade figured with a hundred flowers, a coat of linked mail with beast faces at the shoulders, and a jewelled belt with lions worked upon it drawn tight over the armor; bow and arrows at his side, the crescent-bladed halberd in his hand, and under him [Red Hare](misc-red-hare), that neighs into the wind. Truly: among men, Lü Bu; among horses, Red Hare!
[Wang Kuang](char-wang-kuang) turned his head. "Who will go out against him?" A general behind him put his horse forward with his spear levelled, and Wang Kuang saw that it was Fang Yue, a noted man of Henei. The horses closed, and before five bouts [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu)'s halberd had him out of the saddle; then Lü Bu levelled it and charged straight on. Wang Kuang's army broke and ran every way, and Lü Bu drove east and west among them as though he rode through empty air. By good luck the two forces of [Qiao Mao](char-qiao-mao) and [Yuan Yi](char-yuan-yi) came up to save Wang Kuang, and at that Lü Bu drew off. The three lords, each with some loss of men and horse, fell back thirty li and camped. The other five came up after them, and they took counsel together, agreeing that Lü Bu was a hero no man could match.
While they were still at their fears, a junior officer brought word: "[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) is challenging us to battle." The eight lords mounted together and drew their men up in eight bodies on the high ground, and saw far off Lü Bu's company of horse, with embroidered banners fluttering, come on ahead to break their line. Mu Shun, an officer under [Zhang Yang](char-zhang-yang), Grand Administrator of Shangdang, rode out with his spear levelled to meet him; Lü Bu's hand rose, and the halberd had him out of the saddle. A shock went through them all. Then Wu Anguo, an officer under [Kong Rong](char-kong-rong), Grand Administrator of Beihai, came flying out with an iron hammer, and Lü Bu swung the halberd, clapped heels to his horse and came to meet him. They fought above ten bouts, and then one stroke cut through Wu Anguo's wrist; he dropped the hammer on the ground and ran. The men of the eight armies came out together and brought him off, and Lü Bu drew back. The lords returned to camp and took counsel. "There is no matching Lü Bu's valor," said [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao). "Let the eighteen lords meet and find a good plan between them. Take Lü Bu, and [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) will be easy to kill."
They were still debating when [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) brought his men out again and offered battle, and the eight lords went out together. [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) swung his lance and fought Lü Bu himself; they had not fought a few bouts when he broke and fled, and Lü Bu gave [Red Hare](misc-red-hare) its head and came after him. The horse went a thousand li a day and flew like the wind. He was all but up with him, and raised the halberd to drive it between Gongsun Zan's shoulders, when a general at his side — his great round eyes glaring, his tiger whiskers bristling — levelled the Serpent Spear and came flying up with a shout: "Stand, you slave of three surnames! [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) of Yan is here!"
[Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) saw him, left [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan), and turned upon [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei). Zhang Fei gathered himself and closed with him fiercely; above fifty bouts they fought together, and neither had the better. Then [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) saw it, clapped heels to his horse, and came up swinging the Crescent Blade of eighty-two jin to take Lü Bu on the other side; and the three horses closed in the shape of a T. Thirty bouts more, and Lü Bu was not to be beaten down. Then [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) drew his pair of swords, put his yellow-maned horse to the gallop, and came in slantwise to help them.
The three ringed [Lü Bu](char-lu-bu) round and fought him, wheeling about him like the figures on a turning lantern, and the men of the eight armies stood staring. Lü Bu could hold his guard no longer; he made a feint of the halberd at [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei)'s face, and as Liu Bei dodged aside he broke open a corner of the ring, trailed the halberd behind him, and galloped off. The three would not let him go, but whipped their horses after him. The eight armies raised a great shout and swept forward together, and Lü Bu's people ran for the pass with Liu Bei, [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) at their heels. A man of old wrote a piece on this very fight:
> With Huan and Ling the fate of Han was told;
> The blazing sun leaned westward, red and old.
> The traitor [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) pulled the Emperor down;
> Weak [Liu Xie](char-prince-xie)'s soul took fright beneath the crown.
> [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) sent out his call to all the land;
> The angry lords rose up on every hand.
> [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) by common voice was set at head;
> They swore to prop the throne and peace to spread.
> The Marquis Lü Bu had no peer on earth;
> The four seas praised his greatness and his worth.
> His silver mail was set like dragon scale;
> His golden coronet bore pheasant's tail.
> Beasts gaped upon his belt in golden hue;
> Across his robe a broidered phoenix flew.
> His dragon steed stamped up a wind in flight;
> His halberd glittered cold as autumn light.
> He rode out from the pass: who dared to stay?
> The lords' hearts split, and courage fled away.
> Out leapt Zhang Fei of Yan to bar the road,
> And in his hand the Serpent Spear he showed.
> His tiger whiskers bristled stiff as wire;
> His great round eyes glared open, flashing fire.
> The heated fight made neither side prevail;
> Before the line, Guan Yu felt rage assail.
> Green Dragon's Blade flashed frost before their eyes;
> His parrot-green robe danced with butterflies.
> Where'er his hooves came down the ghosts cried dread;
> Before his rage, a stream of blood was shed.
> Then bold Liu Bei drew either shining blade,
> And all the terror of the heav'ns displayed.
> The three encircled, round him wheeled in style;
> Cut, thrust, and parry ceased not all the while.
> The shouting shook the heavens and the ground;
> The air of slaughter chilled the stars around.
> Lü Bu's strength failed; he looked to flee the plain,
> He spied the far hill fort and turned his rein.
> He trailed the crescent halberd at his side;
> His gold-wrought banners, five-hued, scattered wide.
> He snapped the silken cord, let [Red Hare](misc-red-hare) fly;
> Wheeled in the saddle, soared to [Hulao](loc-hulao-pass) high.
The three chased Lü Bu right to the foot of the pass, and saw a canopy of green silk stirring above it in the west wind. "That must be Dong Zhuo!" shouted Zhang Fei. "What is the good of chasing Lü Bu? Take the traitor Dong first, and we pull the weed up by the root!" And he whipped his horse up toward the pass to take Dong Zhuo. Truly:
> To seize the rebels, their chief must fall;
> Rare feats await the rarest man of all.
How the fight went, the next chapter will tell.
